title: He will come again
hook: the creeds say Christ will return; churches differ on how and when

segments.voice: Yesterday, hell, and the different ways churches hold it. Your line was his mercy is wide. Who got more mercy from you than they'd earned? Day one thousand one hundred nine.

A group of friends stands on a hill, staring at the sky. Jesus has just been taken up out of their sight, and they're still looking. Then two men in white are beside them: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven." The creeds keep that promise. And churches have read it in different ways: some with urgency, some with quiet patience, some with careful timelines. Today's word: he will come again.

The creeds say it in a line. The Apostles' Creed: "From thence he shall come to judge the quick and the dead." The quick means the living. One New Testament Greek word for his coming is parousia: an arrival, a presence. Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches that say the creeds share that hope. Where they differ is how, and when. Revelation speaks of a thousand years in which Christ reigns. Some read that as a future age that begins when he returns. Others read it as now: the time of the church, between his first coming and his second. Some evangelical churches teach that believers will first be caught up to meet him, often called the rapture, drawing on Paul's words about meeting the Lord in the air. Other churches read those same words differently. And the date? Jesus is plain: "But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only." So the stance the Gospels ask for is not calculation but readiness. Jesus tells of servants who keep their lights burning, waiting up for their master. And near the Bible's very end comes a short prayer: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Paul, closing his first letter to Corinth, leaves an Aramaic word untranslated: maranatha. Readers take it two ways: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. Some readers hear both in it: he came, and he will come.

Here's the practice: live today as if he might come. Sit still for a moment, and let your breath settle. Jesus tells of servants with their lights burning, awake when their master knocks. Not frightened. Ready. So ask, quietly: if today were the day, what would I want to have done? Who would I call? What would I put down? What would I finish? Let one answer come clearly. If you pray, you can use the prayer near the Bible's end: even so, come, Lord Jesus. If you don't, just hold the question. The bell holds the time.
He will come again. The creeds' promise that Christ will return to judge the living and the dead. Churches share the promise, and differ on how and when.
Your line: come, Lord Jesus. Today, do the one thing you'd most want done if this were the last ordinary day. Day one thousand one hundred nine.

howItsDone: Christians who say the Apostles' or Nicene Creed confess that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and the season of Advent looks toward his coming; churches differ on how they read the details in Revelation and Paul.

trapdoor: what you thought: a doomsday prediction with a date on it.

notes: Index hook says 'all churches say Christ will return'; this script says 'churches that say the creeds share that hope' instead of 'all'.

Millennial views summarized as future age (premillennial) vs. present church age (amillennial); postmillennialism omitted. 'Some evangelical churches teach... the rapture' is uncounted. Confirm fairness.
Parousia glossed as 'an arrival, a presence'; other NT words (epiphaneia, apokalypsis) also used, hence 'one'. Confirm.
Maranatha: the two readings (μαράνα θά 'our Lord, come' / μαρὰν ἀθά 'our Lord has come') depend on word division; confirm wording. Not given in Greek script to avoid a spelling guess.
'People have tried to set dates anyway, and the dates have come and gone' gives no names or numbers; confirm acceptable.
Apostles' Creed line: confirm BCP 1662 wording and capitalization.

Editor: cut 'people have tried to set dates anyway, and the dates have come and gone' (a historical claim no cited text makes); 'the Bible's very last pages end with' and 'the Bible's last prayer' became 'near the Bible's end' (Revelation 22:21 follows 22:20); 'lamps' changed to 'lights' to match Luke 12:35; maranatha readings and the trapdoor's echo attributed to readers.

Auditor: "some with charts" read as a jab at churches that map prophecy; reworded neutrally. "Both fit. He came. He will come." had the narrator asserting the belief; now attributed to readers. Acts 1:11, Matthew 24:36, Revelation 22:20 and the BCP 1662 Apostles' Creed line checked.
